strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: measuring degrees of human informational contribution in AI-assisted writing. Its distinction between informational contribution, human effort, and legal authorship is useful.

The proposed prompt-aware statistic is computationally simple, requires no additional training, and has explicit token-likelihood formulas. The manuscript provides a code link, model identifiers, dataset sources, and computational details.

The experiments cover four domains, 2,000 source documents per domain, multiple models, and five generations per input. The consistent ordering across prompting conditions supports the statistic’s sensitivity to differences in supplied information.
Human pairwise judgments, 2,500 WildChat examples, surrogate-model experiments, and length, temperature, and multi-round analyses provide useful evidence beyond a single synthetic setting.
weaknesses: The central interpretation as a percentage of human-contributed information is insufficiently justified. Equations 1–5 calculate normalized log-likelihood gain, but the no-prompt likelihood is not shown to equal the output marginal under a distribution of human prompts, as the mutual-information interpretation requires. Furthermore, pointwise mutual information can be negative; Figure 7 contains negative scores even when the input is available. These issues undermine the nonnegative shared-information decomposition illustrated in Figure 1 and require clarification before scores can be interpreted as contribution percentages.

The text-only extension does not establish the minimum claimed in Definition 2. Equation 9 supplies a lower bound under the chosen plausibility constraint, whereas Equation 10 treats that bound as the minimum without demonstrating attainability or tightness. Moreover, Equation 10 equals 1 + log(τ)/(I(y)/N), so for a fixed model and threshold its ranking is exactly a monotone transformation of per-token surprisal. The reported ordinal trends therefore do not independently validate minimum-contribution estimation. Threshold selection, sensitivity, and whether actual generating prompts satisfy the constraint need evaluation.

The validation supports separation of prompting regimes more clearly than quantitative contribution measurement. Content, summary, title, and subject conditions differ substantially in input length and copying opportunity, yet there are no comparisons with length ratios, lexical or semantic overlap, or likelihood-based baselines. The reported 97.4% human agreement uses only pairs whose proposed scores differ by more than 0.1, leaving performance on unfiltered, closely scored, and within-condition comparisons unresolved. WildChat class differences also provide only coarse proxy validation. Independent comparisons and controls are needed to establish what the measure adds beyond these confounds.

The adaptive-attack evidence is limited to two fixed instructions concerning rare words and human-like writing. Neither procedure demonstrably adapts to feedback from the proposed metric, and no optimization budget or attack-success criterion is reported. These experiments support robustness to the tested instructions, but broader resilience claims need stronger evaluation.

Reproducibility cannot be adequately assessed from the supplied PDF. Essential sampling details, generation prompts, and annotation instructions are deferred to supplementary material that is not included. Annotator counts, agreement, and blinding are not reported here; likelihood-scoring templates and treatment of decoding temperature also need specification. The Mistral/Mixtral naming inconsistency further obscures the surrogate-model setup. The public code link is helpful, but these omissions, together with the central validity gaps, prevent a Findings recommendation in the current form.
